authentication.title: Authentication
authentication.summary: How user identity is verified across the system: mostly server-side Google ID token validation, with one Azure EasyAuth exception.

body.overview: Most backend services validate a Google ID token themselves, server-side, on every request — no session state, no cookies, just a Bearer token checked against Google's public keys. ideas-api is the one exception: it delegates token validation to Azure's EasyAuth layer instead of doing it in application code.

sections.heading: Google ID token (application-level)
sections.content: posts-api and learning-plan-api both validate the caller's Google ID token themselves, in application code, via the google-auth library — checking the token's signature and audience against one or more configured Google OAuth client IDs. This is the default pattern for any new backend service: no Azure-specific auth wiring, works identically whether the caller is the web app or a CLI tool, and keeps auth logic visible and testable in the service's own codebase rather than delegated to platform configuration.

sections.heading: Azure EasyAuth (platform-level)
sections.content: ideas-api instead relies on Azure Functions' built-in EasyAuth: Azure validates the Google ID token at the platform layer before the request ever reaches application code, then injects the validated identity as a request header. This means less code in ideas-api itself, but the auth behavior lives in Azure Function App configuration rather than in the repo — a real tradeoff worth knowing before assuming "how auth works" from reading the code alone.

sections.heading: General philosophy
sections.content: Prefer application-level Google ID token validation for new services — it's portable, testable, and doesn't depend on Azure-specific platform configuration a future migration would need to reproduce. EasyAuth is not being actively adopted further; it's a historical choice on ideas-api, not the recommended pattern going forward.
